newsitem.title: UK: LPC-Japan premium's impact on Euroloans seen muted.
newsitem.headline: LPC-Japan premium's impact on Euroloans seen muted.

text.p: LONDON, Jan 29 (LPC) - Despite a recent increase in the cost of funding for Japanese banks, there is little fear among syndicators that the Japanese might cut back severely from the Euroloan market.

A slump in the Tokyo stock market has reignited concerns about the health of the Japanese banking system and caused a spike in the so-called Japan premium - the extra cost of funding for Japanese banks in non-yen currencies.
Earlier on Wednesday major Japanese banks were paying a premium of about 19 basis points over the prevailing three-month Eurodollar deposit rate.
Though such a premium means that many Japanese banks would currently be funding thinly-priced Euroloans at a loss, the consensus among bankers is that so far it has had minimal effect on the market.

One banker at a top Japanese bank admitted that they had in the past done deals where the premium to borrow funds had exceeded the margin, but said that maintaining long-term relationships was the important thing.
The premium has gone up and down over the past year, he said, "But we would never pull out of the market because of the premium."

As Japanese banks provide 10 to 15 per cent of the liquidity in the Euroloan market, a pullback by them could make credit "I think the top banks learned their lesson eight or nine years ago when some Japanese banks withdrew and they lost a lot of their relationship business," said a syndicator with major European bank.
"My overriding feeling is that they will continue to do whatever it takes to protect their positions in the market," said a British banker.

Other bankers agreed: "Major Japanese players in the international markets cannot afford to withdraw. The relationship takes time to develop and they need to stay in the market and arrange deals to enhance their yields on the lending that they are doing,"said one.
If any banks do pull back from European lending, it is likely to be from among the second tier of Japanese banks which participate at relatively low levels, bankers said.
"I've only seen an impact with smaller Japanese banks," said a banker at an American bank.
"They particularly have trouble with deals in more unusual currencies, they hate ECU and Swiss franc deals," he added.
"I already know that there are some second tier Japanese banks that will not do anything for a margin of less than 15 bps," said one banker at a Japanese institution.

One banker at an American house went so far as to suggest that this would be the issue that turns pricing around: "Whatever happens this will raise pricing and a strong single 'A' borrower will no longer be able to borrow at 15 bps but will be looking at paying 17.5 bps to 18.75."

But most bankers spoken to said that any withdrawal by smaller Japanese banks would have little impact on the overall market since there is so much excess liquidity as French and German borrowers increase their activity.
